problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:** I have successfully solved the problem. The final answer is \(\boxed{4048}\).

**b. Method Sketch:**  
1. **Structure of uncovered squares.**  
   Since each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered squares are \(\{(i,\pi(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}\).

2. **Critical cells.**  
   For every uncovered square \((i,\pi(i))\) define the *right‑adjacent* cell \((i,\pi(i)+1)\) when \(\pi(i)<n\) and the *below‑adjacent* cell \((i+1,\pi(i))\) when \(i<n\).  
   Exactly one uncovered square lies in the last column and one in the last row, so the total number of defined critical cells is \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\).

3. **Key Lemma.**  
   *Lemma.* Any axis‑aligned rectangular tile that avoids all uncovered squares can contain **at most one** critical cell.  
   *Proof.* Suppose a rectangle \(R\) contains two distinct critical cells. Three cases are possible:  
   - two right‑adjacent cells,  
   - two below‑adjacent cells,  
   - one right‑adjacent and one below‑adjacent cell.  
   In each case a simple geometric argument shows that a hole (an uncovered square) must also lie inside \(R\), contradicting the definition of a tile. Hence a tile cannot contain two critical cells.

4. **Lower bound.**  
   Because each tile can cover at most one critical cell and there are \(2n-2\) critical cells, any tiling must use at least \(2n-2\) tiles.

5. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\); the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).  
   - For each \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\) place a horizontal rectangle covering row \(i\) and columns \(i+1,\dots ,n\).  
   - For each \(j=1,\dots ,n-1\) place a vertical rectangle covering column \(j\) and rows \(j+1,\dots ,n\).  
   These \( (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) rectangles are pairwise disjoint, avoid all diagonal holes, and together cover every other unit square.

6. **Conclusion.**  
   The universal lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles show that the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\). For \(n=2025\) this equals \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
A placement of tiles satisfying the condition “each row and each column has exactly one uncovered unit square’’ forces the set of uncovered squares to be a permutation matrix.  
Hence there exists a permutation \(\pi\colon\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that

\[
H=\{(i,\pi(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}
\]

is precisely the set of uncovered squares.  
All other unit squares must belong to pairwise disjoint axis‑aligned rectangular tiles whose sides lie on grid lines.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1. Critical cells

For each \((i,\pi(i))\in H\) define

\[
R_i=
\begin{cases}
(i,\pi(i)+1), & \text{if }\pi(i)<n,\\[2mm]
\text{undefined}, & \text{if }\pi(i)=n,
\end{cases}
\qquad
D_i=
\begin{cases}
(i+1,\pi(i)), & \text{if }i<n,\\[2mm]
\text{undefined}, & \text{if }i=n .
\end{cases}
\]

\(R_i\) is the unit square immediately to the right of the hole in row \(i\); \(D_i\) is the unit square immediately below the hole in column \(\pi(i)\).  

Because exactly one hole lies in the last column, there is exactly one index \(i_0\) with \(\pi(i_0)=n\); for this index \(R_{i_0}\) is undefined.  
Similarly, because exactly one hole lies in the last row, there is exactly one index \(j_0\) with \(\pi(j_0)=j\) for some \(j\); for this index \(D_{j_0}\) is undefined.  

Consequently the set of defined critical cells

\[
C=\{R_i\mid \pi(i)<n\}\cup\{D_i\mid i<n\}
\]

has cardinality

\[
|C|=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2. Lemma: a tile contains at most one critical cell

\[
\textbf{Lemma.}\quad\text{Let }T\text{ be a rectangle (product of a row interval and a column interval) that contains no hole. Then }|T\cap C|\le 1.
\]

*Proof.*  
Write \(T=[a,b]\times[c,d]\) with integer bounds \(1\le a\le b\le n\) and \(1\le c\le d\le n\).  
Assume for contradiction that \(T\) contains two distinct critical cells. Three possibilities arise.

1. **Two right‑adjacent cells.**  
   Suppose \((i,\pi(i)+1)\) and \((j,\pi(j)+1)\) belong to \(T\) with \(i\neq j\).  
   Then \(a\le i,j\le b\) and \(c\le \pi(i)+1,\pi(j)+1\le d\).  
   Let \(L=\min\{\pi(i)+1,\pi(j)+1\}\) and \(R=\max\{\pi(i)+1,\pi(j)+1\}\).  
   Hence the whole column interval \([L,R]\) lies inside \([c,d]\).  
   The column of the hole \((i,\pi(i))\) equals \(\pi(i)=L-1\) or \(\pi(i)\ge L\).  
   Since the holes \((i,\pi(i))\) and \((j,\pi(j))\) occupy distinct columns, they cannot both equal \(L-1\).  
   Therefore at least one of the holes has column \(\ge L\) and thus lies in \([c,d]\); its row lies in \([a,b]\).  
   Consequently that hole lies inside \(T\), contradicting the hypothesis that \(T\) avoids all holes.

2. **Two below‑adjacent cells.**  
   This case is symmetric to the previous one after interchanging the roles of rows and columns; the same argument yields a contradiction.

3. **One right‑adjacent and one below‑adjacent cell.**  
   Suppose \((i,\pi(i)+1)\) and \((j+1,\pi(j))\) belong to \(T\).  
   Then \(a\le i\le b\), \(a\le j+1\le b\), \(c\le \pi(i)+1\le d\), and \(c\le \pi(j)\le d\).

   - If \(i=j\), then rows \(i,i+1\) and columns \(\pi(i),\pi(i)+1\) are all contained in \(T\); hence the hole \((i,\pi(i))\) lies in \(T\), a contradiction.

   - If \(i\neq j\), assume without loss of generality \(i<j\) (otherwise exchange the two cells).  
     Then rows \(i,i+1,\dots ,j+1\) are all in \([a,b]\); in particular row \(j\) belongs to \([a,b]\).  

     Compare the two column numbers \(\pi(i)+1\) and \(\pi(j)\).

     *If \(\pi(i)+1\le \pi(j)\):* column \(\pi(j)\) lies in \([c,d]\) and row \(j\) lies in \([a,b]\); thus the hole \((j,\pi(j))\) belongs to \(T\).

     *If \(\pi(i)+1>\pi(j)\):* then \(\pi(i)=\pi(i)+1-1\ge \pi(j)\), so column \(\pi(i)\) lies in \([c,d]\) and row \(i\) lies in \([a,b]\); thus the hole \((i,\pi(i))\) belongs to \(T\).

     In either subcase a hole lies inside \(T\), contradicting the hypothesis.

Since all possibilities lead to a contradiction, a rectangle avoiding holes can contain at most one critical cell. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3. Lower bound on the number of tiles

Every tile is a rectangle that avoids all holes; by the Lemma each tile can cover at most one critical cell.  
Because there are exactly \(2n-2\) critical cells by (1), any tiling must use at least

\[
\boxed{2n-2}
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4. Construction attaining the bound

Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) for all \(i\).  
The uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\), \(i=1,\dots ,n\).

Define the following rectangles:

*For each \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\)*
\[
H_i=\{(i,j)\mid j=i+1,i+2,\dots ,n\},
\]
a horizontal rectangle of size \(1\times (n-i)\).

*For each \(j=1,\dots ,n-1\)*
\[
V_j=\{(i,j)\mid i=j+1,j+2,\dots ,n\},
\]
a vertical rectangle of size \((n-j)\times 1\).

The families \(\{H_i\}\) and \(\{V_j\}\) are pairwise disjoint:  
\(H_i\) occupies precisely those squares with row index \(i\) and column index \(>i\);  
\(V_j\) occupies precisely those squares with column index \(j\) and row index \(>j\).  
Thus no square belongs to both a horizontal and a vertical rectangle.

Every non‑diagonal square either satisfies column > row (hence lies in a unique \(H_i\)) or row > column (hence lies in a unique \(V_j\)).  
Consequently the union of all \(H_i\) and \(V_j\) covers all unit squares except the diagonal holes \((i,i)\).

The total number of rectangles used is
\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2.
\]

Thus a tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5. Minimality

The universal lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit construction achieving this number show that the minimum possible number of tiles is precisely \(2n-2\).

For the given board with \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4050-2 = \boxed{4048}.
\]
